performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
intro: This movement shows gossip at the market in Limoges about a missing cow, new false teeth and a conspicuously red nose. Mussorgsky set the chatter in quick notes, and Ravel’s orchestration passes them between violins and woodwinds.

sections.label: A · Violins in quick repeated notes
sections.mNote: Quick repeated notes centre on B♭, in E♭ major.

sections.label: B · Three-beat bars, D major chords
sections.mNote: D major chords; the metre soon changes to three beats.

sections.label: A′ · Opening E♭ material again
sections.mNote: A descending chromatic bass brings back the opening phrase.

sections.label: Coda · Four bars leading to the catacombs
sections.mNote: A fermata, then Meno mosso and a final acceleration.

cues.title: Opening phrase, violins
cues.text: The violins open with a phrase in semiquavers. Woodwinds take it up, horns add accented interjections and the celesta joins in. Mussorgsky marked the movement sempre scherzando, and accents fall throughout the semiquaver figuration.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 1–11; Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, 7 April 2022, p. 7: https://philharmonia-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2022/04/07.04.22_RFH-online.pdf. Ravel attribution for this recording remains inferred.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Crossed-out programme, manuscript, 1874
cues.text: In his 1874 manuscript Mussorgsky wrote out the market’s news in French. A man has recovered his cow, a woman has acquired porcelain teeth, and another man’s nose remains as red as a peony. He later crossed the passage out.
cues.evidence: Peter Laki quotes the crossed-out manuscript programme: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition-mussorgsky. Michael Steinberg gives another translation: https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition

cues.title: Final bars, Meno mosso
cues.text: A fermata stops the movement. The last four bars are marked Meno mosso, with a slower pulse and shorter notes, semidemiquavers passed across the orchestra. The score accelerates at the end and continues without a break into the Catacombs.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 36–40: fermata, Meno mosso, sempre capriccioso, semidemiquavers, poco accelerando and attacca: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/MussorgskyM/pictures-at-an-exhibition/pictures-at-an-exhibition-lys/limoges.ly
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: E♭ to D major at bar 12
transitions.from: A · Violins in quick repeated notes
transitions.to: B · Three-beat bars, D major chords
transitions.how: The E♭ phrase ends, and at bar 12 a D major chord (D–F♯–A), with F♯ in the bass, begins the middle passage. The key signature is cleared at this point, and the harmony is D major. The semiquavers continue. From bar 16 the bars shorten from four beats to three, so each new accent comes round more quickly.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 11–16: D–F♯–A chord at bar 12, three-beat metre from bar 16. The empty key signature at bar 12 accompanies D major harmony, not C major.

transitions.title: A chromatic slide back to E♭
transitions.from: B · Three-beat bars, D major chords
transitions.how: Repeated Ds continue to the end of the middle passage in bars 25–27. Beneath them the bass descends in semitones from C♯ to E♭, with a diminuendo. The opening E♭ phrase then returns, marked mf, still in semiquavers.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 25–27: repeated D, descending chromatic bass, diminuendo and E♭ return marked mf; Mutopia transcription.

transitions.title: Fermata, Meno mosso, then attacca
transitions.to: Coda · Four bars leading to the catacombs
transitions.how: Three accented figures end in a rest under a fermata. Meno mosso, sempre capriccioso then begins over B♭ in the bass, with E♭ major chords broken into semidemiquavers (bars 36–40 in Lamm’s edition). The last bar accelerates and rises chromatically, and attacca leads straight into the catacombs.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 36–40, including the bass B♭, E♭ major chords and final chromatic ascent; Mutopia transcription.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (1:40; this file is 1:40), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No venue is documented. The Free Music Archive biography describes the orchestra as a semi-professional ensemble of Skidmore students and regional professionals; this is not a recording location.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The original release is not identified; Musopen and the Free Music Archive are distribution channels.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix, take or side identifiers are supplied.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified; the uploader of the Commons file (Raul654) is not assumed to be one.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: Upload dates are not transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No processing is disclosed. The access file is a Wikimedia MP3 derivative of the uploaded Ogg Vorbis file.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. The Internet Archive copy of the first Promenade is marked CC0 1.0. Session date is not needed for this route.

composer.epithet: He could make a singer sound like a frightened child, a drunken monk or a tsar who could no longer bear his own thoughts.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition with Mily Balakirev, outside the conservatory
Guards officer until 1858; later a clerk in the Forestry Department and Government Control
Borodin, Cui, Balakirev, Rimsky-Korsakov; Vladimir Stasov and Viktor Hartmann
Boris Godunov, unfinished operas, three song cycles, Pictures at an Exhibition
composer.background:
When Borodin met Mussorgsky at a Saint Petersburg military hospital in 1856, the seventeen-year-old officer was immaculate, with a close-fitting uniform, polished manners and well-kept hands. He played extracts from Il trovatore and La traviata at the piano while admirers gathered round. Twenty-five years later, in another hospital, Repin painted the portrait that became his most familiar likeness. It shows a man in a dressing gown, his hair in disorder and his eyes still alert.

Mussorgsky was born at Karevo, on his family’s estate. His mother taught him the piano, and his nurse’s stories prompted the improvisations he remembered from childhood. At ten he was sent to school in Saint Petersburg, where he studied piano with Anton Gerke. He entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852 and received a commission in the Preobrazhensky Regiment in 1856. His father paid for the publication of his first piano piece, a polka.
